rows.verified: Employers must make sure workers receive immediate help if they are injured or become ill at work.
Employers should complete a first-aid needs assessment that reflects the particular circumstances of the workplace.
Every workplace must have a suitably stocked first-aid kit.
Provision should include an appointed person or suitable numbers of appropriately trained first-aiders, as identified by the needs assessment.
All employees must be told about the workplace first-aid arrangements.

rows.source: HSE first aid frequently asked questions
rows.verified: An appointed person takes charge of first-aid arrangements, looks after equipment and facilities and calls emergency services when required.

rows.source: HSE first aid frequently asked questions
rows.verified: An appointed person does not need first-aid training solely to fulfil the appointed-person role.
First-aid needs assessment should consider workplace circumstances and current guidance also emphasises workers' mental health and identified risks of life-threatening bleeding.
First-aid provision depends on workforce size, hazards, work patterns, remoteness, vulnerable people, accident history and access to emergency services.
First-aid evidence is workplace-, workforce- and hazard-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury-outcome probability.
Employers must manage health and safety risks before employees, contractors or self-employed people work alone.
Lone workers work without close or direct supervision and may include drivers, health workers, engineers, cleaners, security staff and homeworkers.
Employers must train, supervise and monitor lone workers, keep in touch and respond to incidents.
When a lone worker visits another employer's workplace, relevant risks and control measures should be obtained from that employer.
Lone-working assessments should consider violence, stress, mental health, medical suitability and isolated or rural locations.
Some high-risk work requires another person, including certain confined-space, live-electrical, diving, explosives-transport and fumigation activities.
The same health and safety responsibilities apply to homeworkers, including supervision, training and sufficient controls.
Lone-working arrangements should recognise that direct help may not be available when something goes wrong.
Lone-working controls depend on the task, location, worker, communication method, supervision, travel, violence risk and emergency response.
Lone-working evidence is worker-, task- and location-specific and is not an exact parcel-level incident probability.
